cards.explanation: The answer is Shepherd. Asaph sings, “Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock…” A flock needs somebody out front, and that's the name he reaches for. Sheep don't pick their own route, friends, and I know a few stamper-shaped folks who get lost in a kitchen. Good to have a Shepherd who leads.

The answer is that God would rally His power and come save them. Asaph prays, “Rally Your mighty power and come to save us.” He doesn't ask God to send help from a distance. He asks God to come Himself. That's a man who knows exactly who he's calling.

The answer is True. Asaph prays, “Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.” The last part of the sentence is the reason he gives for the asking. Saved is where this prayer is headed, friends.

The answer is God's anger smoldering against their prayers. Asaph asks, “O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?” Smolder is a good word, because it's a slow burn and not a blaze. And notice whose prayers these are: His own people's. That's the question hanging over the whole song.

The answer is bread of tears and tears to drink. Asaph says, “You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears.” Tears for the meal and tears for the drink. I think that's a song written by someone who has cried a lot, and the verse is heavy.

The answer is mock. Asaph says, “You make us contend with our neighbors; our enemies mock us.” Mocking stings in its own way, friends. I've heard my share of jokes about a stamper with a mustache for hands, but I got to laugh along. That's a different kind of mocking than this verse.

The answer is Egypt. Asaph sings, “You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it.” Egypt is the place God pulled the vine up from. And God does the pulling up and the planting Himself.

The answer is False. Asaph says, “You drove out the nations and transplanted it.” The land had nations in it, and God drove them out before the vine went in. It's the one thing the verse spells out about where the vine got planted.

The answer is root. Asaph says of the vine, “You cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land.” Roots first, then everything else. Plants don't skip that step. The ground was cleared and the vine took root.
The answer is the Sea. Asaph says, “It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River.” The vine reaches all the way to the Sea. That's a vine with ambition, friends.

The answer is False. Asaph asks, “Why have You broken down its walls, so that all who pass by pick its fruit?” He's speaking to God, and he says “You.” The verse never says enemies knocked the walls down. That's why it's such a heavy WHY.

The answer is a boar. Asaph says, “The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed upon it.” It's a boar, and it comes out of the forest. With the walls down, nothing's keeping it out.

The answer is heaven. Asaph prays, “Return, O God of Hosts, we pray! Look down from heaven and see! Attend to this vine…” Return, look, attend: he stacks up the asks fast. I think he's piling them on because he's desperate, and I'd pray just as fast with smoke pouring out of my oven.

The answer is at God's right hand. Asaph prays, “Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand, on the son of man You have raised up for Yourself.” The man is at God's right hand, and Asaph says God raised him up for Himself. That's the place the verse names, friends.
The answer is True. Asaph says, “Then we will not turn away from You; revive us, and we will call on Your name.” The people say they will not turn away from God. It's a promise inside a prayer.
The answer is that they will call on His name. Asaph says, “revive us, and we will call on Your name.” That's what he promises if God revives them. I think it's a lovely thing to promise, friends.
